extraction_text: King Janaka of Mithila asks the sage Parashara about the highest truth, seeking definitions of supreme bliss, the ultimate goal, indestructible actions, and the path from which one does not return.

attributes.relationship: King Janaka seeks spiritual guidance from Sage Parashara.

extraction_text: Sage Parashara explains that non-attachment is the foundation of supreme bliss, knowledge is the highest path, and perfected austerities and proper charity are indestructible.

key_points: Perfected austerities and proper charity as indestructible

extraction_text: Parashara teaches that cutting off bonds of unrighteousness, loving righteousness, and granting fearlessness to all beings leads to supreme achievement.
Parashara contrasts the wise who remain unattached to sense objects with the foolish who indulge in them, using similes of water on lotus leaves and resin on wood.

similes: Wise unattached like water on lotus leaves
Foolish attached like resin on wood

extraction_text: Parashara explains that unrighteous actions inevitably return to their doer, while the self-realized person who understands cause and effect remains unharmed.

key_points: Self-realized person understands cause and effect

extraction_text: Parashara describes how those with uncontrolled senses who cling to good and bad deeds fall into great terror, while those free from passion and anger remain unstained even among sense objects.

Parashara uses multiple similes (dam, jewel absorbing sunlight, sesame with flowers) to illustrate how righteousness leads to merit growth, yoga operates through meditation, and purity enhances goodness.

Parashara teaches that abandoning worldly attachments (wife, wealth, vehicles, enterprises) and freeing wisdom from sense objects leads to liberation, while attachment to sense objects traps one like a fish with bait.

key_points: Attachment traps like fish with bait

extraction_text: Parashara describes the impermanent nature of the human world (like hollow banana tree, sinking ship) and the uncertainty of life with death always approaching.
Parashara explains liberation through the mind, comparing it to a blind person moving freely at home through habit and a lotus stalk quickly freeing itself from mud.

similes: Mind liberation like blind person at home
Soul liberation like lotus from mud

extraction_text: Parashara concludes that wise souls attain highest heaven through good deeds while foolish souls become lowly animals through bad deeds, and that true happiness comes from renouncing sense enjoyment.

key_points: Wise attain heaven through good deeds
Foolish become animals through bad deeds
True happiness requires renouncing sense enjoyment

extraction_text: King Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the worldly praise for honesty, tolerance, self-control, and wisdom.
Bhishma responds by recounting an ancient dialogue between the Sadhyas and a golden swan.
The eternal, unborn Prajapati manifests as a golden swan and roams the three worlds, encountering the Sadhyas.

attributes.supernatural_element: Prajapati takes form as a golden swan

extraction_text: The Sadhyas, identifying themselves as deities, ask the golden swan for instruction on liberation, inquiring what it considers most excellent and what it holds dear.
The birds ask the swan to teach them the most important good deed that can quickly free a person from all bonds.
The swan responds with teachings on virtues and self-control.
The swan advises against harmful speech and teaches the importance of tolerance.

key_points: Don't seek teachings from unworthy people
Don't speak words that lead to hell

extraction_text: The swan explains the value of non-retaliation and patience.

key_points: Acquiring others' good karma through tolerance

extraction_text: The swan teaches the essence of Vedic wisdom: truth leads to self-restraint, which leads to liberation.
The swan describes the qualities of a true Brahmin and sage.

key_points: Controls impulses of speech, mind, anger, desire, appetite, and lust

extraction_text: The swan explains how not responding to insults benefits the tolerant person.

key_points: Non-retaliation acquires the insulter's good karma
Gods admire those who don't retaliate
Success comes to those who tolerate insults from all

extraction_text: The swan shares personal practices of serving the virtuous and avoiding anger.
The swan uses metaphors to illustrate spiritual progress.

key_points: Wise person sheds sins like moon sheds clouds
Self-restrained person is praised like a tree stump at well

extraction_text: The swan concludes with warnings about anger destroying spiritual merit.

key_points: Angry person loses all merit from sacrifices, charity, austerity, and fire offerings
Yama (god of death) takes everything from angry person

extraction_text: The text presents a dialogue between the Sādhyas (celestial beings) and a swan (Hamsa), discussing moral principles and the qualities of a Brahmin.

attributes.relationships: Sādhyas ask questions, Hamsa provides answers as a wise figure.

extraction_text: The Sādhyas ask four questions about what blinds people, what causes loss of friends, what prevents ascension to heaven, and the unique qualities of a Brahmin.
Hamsa answers that ignorance blinds people, envy dims their light, greed causes loss of friends, and attachment prevents ascension to heaven.
Hamsa further explains that among Brahmins, only the wise are always happy, can remain silent in crowds, have strength even when weak, and avoid quarrels.
Hamsa defines the divine, virtuous, vicious, and human aspects of Brahmins as: studying Vedas (divine), keeping vows (virtuous), slandering (vicious), and death (human).
Bhishma concludes by stating he has narrated the wonderful dialogue between the Sādhyas and Hamsa, emphasizing that the body is the source of action and virtue is truth.

attributes.relationships: Bhishma is the narrator of this dialogue from the Mahabharata.
